questions.stem: Statutory interpretation is the process by which:
options: parliament reads a bill aloud three times in each of its Houses before it can be passed
the Governor-General checks that a bill is constitutional before giving assent
lawyers explain the law to their clients before a case comes before the court
judges give meaning to the words of an Act of parliament when applying it to a case
questions.explanation: Statutory interpretation is the courts deciding what the words of legislation mean so they can apply them to the facts of a case. The readings of a bill are part of parliament's law-making process, not interpretation by a court.

questions.stem: An Act passed in 1985 bans ‘vehicles’ from a park. A court must now decide whether an electric scooter is a vehicle. Which reason for statutory interpretation does this best illustrate?
options: Circumstances have arisen that parliament did not foresee when it passed the Act
The Act has been declared invalid by the High Court under section 109
The Act was passed by parliament without receiving royal assent
The Act conflicts with a precedent set by a lower court in the hierarchy
questions.explanation: Electric scooters did not exist as they do now in 1985, so parliament could not have foreseen whether they would count as vehicles, and the court must decide. Nothing suggests the Act is invalid or lacks assent.

questions.stem: An Act refers to a person who is ‘in charge of’ a vehicle, and the parties argue over whether this includes someone asleep in the driver's seat. Which reason for statutory interpretation is shown?
options: The Act was written in Latin and the court must translate it into plain English
The Act is inconsistent with the Constitution and the court must rewrite it in full
The words of the Act are ambiguous and can reasonably bear more than one meaning
The Act deals with a residual power that the court must transfer to the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: Statutory interpretation is needed when words are ambiguous or unclear, as with ‘in charge of’ here. Courts do not rewrite legislation; they decide what the words mean in the case before them.

questions.stem: In interpreting an unclear Victorian Act, a judge reads the minister's second reading speech to find what the Act was meant to achieve. Why is the judge allowed to do this?
options: Victorian law prefers an interpretation that promotes the purpose of the Act and permits extrinsic material to be considered
Victorian law requires judges to apply the literal meaning of every word, so the speech must replace the Act's original words
Victorian law requires judges to ask the minister personally what the Act means before deciding a case
Victorian law allows judges to ignore an Act completely when a minister's speech contradicts it
questions.explanation: The Interpretation of Legislation Act 1984 (Vic) prefers a construction that promotes the Act's purpose and allows extrinsic material, such as second reading speeches, to help find that purpose. The words of the Act still govern; the speech is only an aid.

questions.stem: What is one effect of a court's statutory interpretation?
options: It may set a precedent for how the words must be interpreted by lower courts in future cases
It changes the wording of the Act, which is then reprinted to include the judge's new wording
It repeals the Act, so parliament must pass a new law before the matter can be decided
It requires a referendum before the interpretation can take effect for the community
questions.explanation: When a court interprets words in an Act, its interpretation forms a precedent that binds lower courts in the same hierarchy. The words of the Act do not change; only parliament can amend or repeal legislation.

questions.stem: After a court interprets ‘family member’ in an Act more narrowly than parliament intended, parliament amends the Act to include a wider definition. This shows that:
options: parliament is supreme and can override a court's interpretation by passing legislation
the court's interpretation was invalid from the start and must be removed from the law reports
the court has abrogated the Act and parliament has codified its decision
the High Court must first approve any amendment to an Act that has been interpreted
questions.explanation: Parliament can pass legislation that overrides a court's interpretation, which shows the supremacy of parliament. Abrogation refers to parliament overriding common law, and the court's decision was valid when made.

questions.stem: The ratio decidendi of a case is:
options: the legal reasoning behind the decision, which is binding on lower courts in the hierarchy
a comment made by the judge in passing, which other courts may consider but need not follow
a summary of the facts of the case prepared by the parties before the trial begins
the decision of the jury about whether the defendant is liable on the evidence
questions.explanation: The ratio decidendi is the reason for the decision and forms the binding part of a precedent. A comment by the way is obiter dictum, which is only persuasive.

questions.stem: A judge in the Victorian Supreme Court (Court of Appeal) states, while deciding a case, that a different outcome might have applied if the defendant had been a child. This statement is:
options: obiter dictum, and is persuasive only
ratio decidendi, and is binding on all courts
a reversal of a precedent from a lower court
an overruling of a High Court precedent
questions.explanation: A remark about a hypothetical situation that was not needed to decide the case is obiter dictum, so it is persuasive rather than binding. Only the ratio decidendi binds lower courts.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes binding precedent?
options: A lower court in the same hierarchy must follow the ratio of a higher court where the material facts are similar
Every court in Australia must follow the ratio of every other Australian court, whatever its position in the hierarchy
A higher court must follow the ratio of a lower court in the same hierarchy if the material facts are similar
A court must follow any precedent from an overseas court, provided its material facts are reasonably similar
questions.explanation: Binding precedent operates downwards within a hierarchy: lower courts must follow the ratio of higher courts in cases with similar material facts. Overseas and lower-court decisions are at most persuasive.

questions.stem: A Victorian Supreme Court judge considers a decision of the New South Wales Court of Appeal on a similar issue. For the Victorian court, that decision is:
options: binding, because all Australian courts form a single state hierarchy
irrelevant, because courts may not consider any interstate decision
persuasive, because it comes from a court in a different hierarchy
binding, because it comes from an appeal court in another state
questions.explanation: Decisions of courts in other state hierarchies are persuasive in Victoria and can influence a judge, but they do not bind. Only the High Court, as the final court of appeal for all Australian courts, binds courts in every hierarchy.

questions.stem: Donoghue v Stevenson (1932) is best known for:
options: establishing the neighbour principle, the basis of the modern law of negligence
establishing that the Commonwealth can implement treaties under the external affairs power
establishing that a person must have standing to challenge the validity of a law
establishing that trials of serious offences without representation may be unfair
questions.explanation: In Donoghue v Stevenson, the House of Lords held that a manufacturer owed a duty of care to the consumer who found the remains of a snail in her ginger beer, establishing the neighbour principle. It was a persuasive precedent later followed in Australian courts.

questions.stem: On appeal, the Court of Appeal changes the decision that the Trial Division of the Supreme Court made in the same case. This is called:
options: reversing the precedent
overruling the precedent
distinguishing the precedent
disapproving the precedent
questions.explanation: Reversing happens when a higher court, on appeal in the same case, changes the lower court's decision. Overruling happens in a later, different case.

questions.stem: In a new and unrelated case, the High Court decides that a precedent it set twenty years earlier was wrong and sets a new one. This is called:
options: reversing
distinguishing
codifying
overruling
questions.explanation: Overruling occurs when a court in a later, different case replaces an earlier precedent. The High Court is not bound by its own previous decisions, so it can overrule itself.

questions.stem: A County Court judge decides that she is not bound by a Court of Appeal precedent because, in her case, the defendant was a qualified professional, unlike the defendant in the earlier case. This is an example of:
options: overruling the precedent, because the County Court is a superior court
reversing the precedent, because the parties in the two cases differ
disapproving the precedent, because the judge has followed it reluctantly
distinguishing the precedent, because the material facts are different
questions.explanation: Distinguishing lets a judge avoid a binding precedent by finding that the material facts are sufficiently different. A County Court judge cannot overrule or reverse a Court of Appeal decision.

questions.stem: A judge follows a binding precedent but says in her judgment that she believes it is wrong and should be reconsidered. Which statement best explains the effect?
options: Disapproving signals concern that may lead a higher court to overrule the precedent later
Disapproving immediately removes the precedent, so it no longer binds any court
Disapproving sends the precedent automatically to parliament for amendment
Disapproving means the judge's decision is invalid and must be appealed
questions.explanation: Disapproving does not change the law at once, because the precedent still binds, but it can influence a higher court to overrule it or prompt parliament to act. The judge's decision is valid and follows the precedent.

questions.stem: For the County Court of Victoria, which of the following is a persuasive rather than binding precedent?
options: The ratio of a Court of Appeal case later affirmed by the High Court
A dissenting judgment in an earlier High Court case
The ratio of an earlier Court of Appeal case with similar material facts
The ratio of an earlier High Court case with similar material facts
questions.explanation: Only the ratio decidendi of the majority binds lower courts, so a dissenting judgment, even in the High Court, is persuasive. Dissents can still matter: a later court may adopt the dissenting reasoning.

questions.stem: Which feature of the doctrine of precedent best allows the common law to stay flexible while remaining consistent?
options: Reversing, as a lower court can change a higher court's decision in a later case
Codification, as a court can rewrite an Act so that it matches an earlier precedent
Binding precedent, as every court can set aside any decision that it disagrees with
Distinguishing, as courts can avoid a precedent where the material facts differ
questions.explanation: Distinguishing lets a court decline to follow a precedent when the material facts are different, so the law can adapt while like cases are still treated alike. Reversing is done by a higher court on appeal in the same case, and codification is done by parliament.

questions.stem: Which is a way that the doctrine of precedent can limit the ability of courts to make law?
options: Courts may only make law when the parties request a new precedent in writing
Courts may only make law in areas of residual power that belong to the states
Lower courts may overrule higher courts only when the law is clearly outdated
Lower courts must follow binding precedents even where they believe the law is outdated
questions.explanation: Because lower courts are bound by higher courts' decisions, they may have to apply a precedent they think is outdated until a higher court or parliament changes it. Lower courts cannot overrule higher courts.

questions.stem: Why does the doctrine of precedent promote consistency in the law?
options: Judges are required to give the same sentence for every offence of the same name
Parliament must approve each precedent before it applies to later cases
Every case must be decided by the High Court so that results are the same
Cases with similar material facts are decided in a similar way, making outcomes predictable
questions.explanation: Precedent means like cases are treated alike, so people can predict how the law will apply and judges are guided by earlier decisions. It does not fix identical sentences, and parliament does not approve precedents.

questions.stem: Judicial conservatism refers to the tendency of judges to:
options: refuse to hear cases involving politically controversial or sensitive topics
follow the views of the government of the day when deciding each of their cases
avoid making major changes to the law, leaving significant reform to parliament
make major changes to the law, believing courts should lead social reform
questions.explanation: Conservative judges are cautious about changing the law and tend to apply existing precedent and the literal words of statutes, leaving big changes to elected parliament. Judges must still decide the cases before them and are independent of government.

questions.stem: A judge says that changing a long-standing rule raises moral issues best left to elected representatives, and applies the existing law. This reflects:
options: the abrogation of common law
the codification of common law
judicial conservatism
judicial activism
questions.explanation: Leaving major moral and social change to parliament is a hallmark of judicial conservatism. An activist judge would be more willing to develop the law in the case to reflect changing values.

questions.stem: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992), in which the High Court rejected terra nullius and recognised native title, is often described as an example of judicial activism. Why?
options: The Court refused to change any law and told parliament it was responsible for deciding the issue of native title
The Court applied the literal words of a statute passed by the Queensland Parliament, without interpreting them
The Court was bound by an earlier native title precedent and applied it because the material facts were the same
The Court departed from long-accepted law to change it significantly in line with justice and contemporary values
questions.explanation: In Mabo the High Court overturned the long-standing assumption that Australia was terra nullius and recognised native title, a major change made by the courts rather than parliament. A conservative court would have left such a change to parliament.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates judicial activism as a factor affecting courts' ability to make law?
options: It means that the courts can make law on any issue they choose, without waiting for a case to come before them
It prevents parliament from changing any law that a court has made, because activist decisions cannot be overridden
It allows courts to update the law to meet changing values, but judges are not elected and may be seen to overstep their role
It ensures that every law made by the courts reflects the views of a majority of voters at the most recent state election
questions.explanation: Activism lets judges develop the law where parliament has not acted, but because they are unelected some argue major change should come from parliament. Courts must still wait for a case, and parliament can override court-made law.

questions.stem: How do costs and time limit the ability of courts to make law?
options: Parties may not take a case to court or appeal, so courts may never get the chance to change the law
Courts may refuse to set a new precedent unless both parties have paid the court's full fees in advance
Judges may only change the law in cases that take less than one year to be heard and decided
Parliament must pay the costs of every case in which a court is likely to set a new precedent
questions.explanation: Courts can only make law when a case comes before them, and the expense and delay of litigation, especially appeals to higher courts, deter many parties. As a result, laws that need changing may not be reviewed by a court.

questions.stem: The requirement for standing means that a person bringing a case must:
options: be represented by a lawyer who has practised before the High Court of Australia
be able to show that their case will create a new precedent for the community
be directly affected by the matter in dispute, having a sufficient interest in it
be an Australian citizen who has lived in the state for at least five years before suing
questions.explanation: To have standing, a plaintiff must be directly affected by the matter or have a sufficient interest in it, not just a general concern. Citizenship and choice of lawyer are not part of the test.

questions.stem: In Australian Conservation Foundation v Commonwealth (1980), the High Court held that the ACF could not challenge a decision about a resort development. What was the reason?
options: The ACF had brought its case to the wrong court and should have gone to the Magistrates' Court
The ACF had already won the same case in a lower court, so the matter had been decided
The ACF's claim had expired under the limitation period that applied to environmental cases
A mere intellectual or emotional concern for the environment did not give the ACF a sufficient interest
questions.explanation: The High Court found that the ACF's concern, however genuine, was intellectual or emotional and did not amount to the special interest needed for standing. The case shows how standing can stop courts from considering issues of public importance.

questions.stem: How does the requirement for standing limit the ability of courts to make law?
options: Courts cannot change a law unless the Attorney-General first agrees that the case can proceed
Courts cannot change a law unless the case has been referred by the Victorian Law Reform Commission
Courts cannot change a law unless a person directly affected brings a case, even if the issue matters to many
Courts cannot change a law unless a jury of twelve has decided that the law is outdated
questions.explanation: Because only those with a sufficient interest can bring a case, interest groups and concerned citizens may be unable to bring a case that would let a court change the law. Juries, the Attorney-General and law reform bodies play no part in this test.

questions.stem: The supremacy of parliament means that:
options: parliament can pass legislation that overrides common law, within the limits of the Constitution
parliament can overrule any High Court decision on the meaning of the Australian Constitution itself
parliament can direct judges on how to decide cases that involve government departments
parliament can pass legislation on any subject at all, regardless of the Constitution
questions.explanation: Parliament is the supreme law-making body and can override common law and courts' interpretations by legislation, but it remains bound by the Constitution. It cannot overrule the High Court's interpretation of the Constitution or direct judges.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why courts are said to have a complementary role to parliament in law-making?
options: Courts must approve each Act before it commences, while parliament interprets the meaning of words
Courts make laws on residual matters, while parliament makes laws on exclusive and concurrent matters
Courts fill gaps and clarify statutes when deciding cases, while parliament makes the broad laws
Courts debate and pass bills in areas parliament cannot, while parliament decides individual cases
questions.explanation: Courts develop the law case by case, through precedent and statutory interpretation, which complements parliament's role as the main law-maker. Courts do not pass bills or approve Acts.

questions.stem: In a judgment, a judge comments that the current law on a particular issue is unjust and should be reviewed by parliament. Parliament later passes a new Act. This best shows:
options: the codification of the common law
the ability of courts to influence parliament
the reversing of a precedent on appeal
the requirement for standing in a case
questions.explanation: Courts can influence parliament by pointing out problems with the law in their judgments, which may prompt legislative reform. Codification is when parliament puts common law into statute, which is not what happened here.

questions.stem: The codification of common law occurs when:
options: parliament passes an Act that confirms a principle developed by the courts
a court reverses a precedent on appeal in the same case before the court
parliament passes an Act that overrides and replaces a common law principle
a court interprets the words of an Act that has been passed by parliament
questions.explanation: Codification is parliament writing a common law principle into statute, giving it the clarity and certainty of legislation. Overriding a common law principle is abrogation.

questions.stem: After the High Court's decision in Mabo (No 2) (1992), the Commonwealth Parliament passed the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), which set out how native title could be recognised and claimed. This is commonly given as an example of:
options: distinguishing a precedent
the requirement for standing
codification of common law
abrogation of common law
questions.explanation: The Native Title Act built on the High Court's recognition of native title and set it out in legislation, which is why it is described as codification. Abrogation would have meant parliament overriding the decision.

questions.stem: In 2005, the Victorian Parliament abolished the common law partial defence of provocation to murder. This is an example of:
options: codification of common law
overruling of a precedent
judicial activism by parliament
abrogation of common law
questions.explanation: Parliament passed legislation that removed a defence developed by the courts, which is abrogation. Overruling can only be done by a court, and activism describes a judge's approach.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes abrogation from codification?
options: Abrogation applies only to criminal law, whereas codification applies only to civil law decided in the courts
Abrogation overrides a common law principle by legislation, whereas codification confirms it in legislation
Abrogation is done by courts reversing parliament, whereas codification is done by parliament reversing courts
Abrogation confirms a common law principle in legislation, whereas codification overrides it by legislation
questions.explanation: Both are done by parliament: abrogation cancels or changes a common law rule, while codification writes it into an Act. Courts cannot abrogate legislation, though they can declare an Act invalid if it breaches the Constitution.

questions.stem: Parliament codifies a common law principle in an Act. Which is a likely later effect?
options: Courts may need to interpret the words of the new Act, so statutory interpretation may develop the law further
Courts will no longer have any role in applying the principle, because parliament itself now decides those cases
Courts will be bound to apply the old precedent and ignore the words used in the new Act
Courts will be prevented from hearing appeals in any cases involving the principle that has been codified
questions.explanation: Once a principle is in an Act, disputes about its words come before courts, which interpret them and may set new precedents. Courts still decide cases, and the Act's words prevail over the earlier precedent.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument that parliament is better placed than the courts to make major changes to the law?
options: Parliament can make laws that apply only to the parties involved in a single dispute
Parliament can consult widely, act on any issue at any time and is accountable to voters
Parliament is bound by precedent, so its laws are always consistent with past court decisions
Parliament must wait for a dispute to arise, so it only acts when a problem is proven
questions.explanation: Parliament can investigate issues through committees and law reform bodies, legislate whenever it chooses and must answer to the electorate. Courts, by contrast, must wait for a case and decide only what is in dispute.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of courts, rather than parliament, making law?
options: Courts can change the law on any topic they choose without needing a case to come before them
Courts are elected by the people, so their decisions reflect the views of the majority
Courts can make sweeping law reforms covering many issues at once in a single judgment
Courts can make a law in response to the facts of a real case, even where parliament has not acted
questions.explanation: Courts can respond to a specific dispute and fill gaps in the law, even when parliament has not addressed an issue. They are limited, however, to the case before them and cannot initiate reform.

questions.stem: Which court sits above the Victorian court hierarchy and can overrule any decision of the Court of Appeal, the highest Victorian court?
options: The Federal Court of Australia
The High Court of Australia
The Supreme Court Trial Division
The County Court of Victoria
questions.explanation: The Court of Appeal, part of the Supreme Court, is the highest Victorian court, but the High Court is a federal court and the final court of appeal for all Australian courts, so it can overrule the Court of Appeal. The Federal Court sits in the federal hierarchy and does not bind Victorian courts.

questions.stem: A lower court must apply a binding precedent from 1960 that reflects outdated values, and neither party can afford an appeal. Which statement best describes the situation?
options: The lower court may overrule the precedent, because it reflects values that are now outdated
The lower court may refer the precedent to the Governor, who can repeal it on the court's advice
The precedent will lapse automatically once it is more than fifty years old
The precedent is likely to remain until parliament changes it, as costs prevent a higher court from reviewing it
questions.explanation: The lower court is bound, and without an appeal no higher court can overrule the precedent, so change may have to come from parliament. Precedents do not expire with age, and only a higher court can overrule one.
